problem: If $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $sin⁡\theta ?$

examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/2262bdc869d10cef3cc7a779365f5afa0eb712676a397e39d248c813b305cbf0.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{3}{4},$ what is the value of $\cos \theta?$
examples.worked_solution:
We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{3}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\cos\theta$ is negative in the third quadrant. So, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac {\sqrt {7}}{4}.$

feedback.problem: The point $P$ is located in the fourth quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $-\frac{5}{9}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $P?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the point $P$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{5}{9}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(-\frac{5}{9})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{25}{81}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{25}{81} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{56}{81} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{56}{81}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $x$ is positive in the fourth quadrant. So our final answer is $x=\frac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.$
